title: The 4% Rule: How Much You Need to Never Work Again
description:
How much money do you need to never work again? The 4% rule gives you a starting point in five seconds: multiply your yearly spending by 25. In this video I explain it from three angles: the numbers (where the rule came from, sequence risk, time horizon, taxes), the psychology of spending your savings, and a five-step playbook to find and reach your own freedom number.

Get The Ryan Rover Money Playbook: [LINK HERE]

11:14 Angle 2: The Psychology
11:30 8. The number makes it real
12:31 9. Fear of spending
13:30 10. Lifestyle creep
14:44 11. One more year syndrome
15:43 12. Freedom without full retirement
16:43 13. Comparison and enough
17:29 14. Uncertainty and flexibility
18:46 Angle 3: The Playbook
18:54 15. Track your real spending
19:56 16. Calculate your freedom number
20:49 17. Factor in Social Security
22:01 18. Close the gap
23:07 19. Protect the early years
24:09 20. Review and adjust
25:01 Three freedom numbers
26:41 Using the rule at every age
27:34 Your freedom number in five steps
29:19 Two retirees
30:28 Questions people ask

33:05 Recap
33:42 What to do next

Sources:
- William P. Bengen, Determining Withdrawal Rates Using Historical Data (Journal of Financial Planning, 1994)
- Cooley, Hubbard and Walz, Retirement Savings: Choosing a Withdrawal Rate That Is Sustainable (AAII Journal, 1998), the Trinity study
- Morningstar, The State of Retirement Income (safe withdrawal rate research)
- Guyton and Klinger, Decision Rules and Maximum Initial Withdrawal Rates (Journal of Financial Planning, 2006)
- Social Security Administration: average retired worker benefit (2025), claiming ages
- Employee Benefit Research Institute: retiree spending and asset drawdown research
- Locke and Latham, goal-setting theory
- Morgan Housel, The Psychology of Money (2020)
- Growth and sequence examples: stated average returns, illustrations, not promises

This video is for education only and is not financial advice. Numbers are illustrations, not promises.
